summary: The DNS server's request-handling pipeline evaluates the access-control policy before name/type transformation and before cache lookup, allowing blocked clients to bypass the policy by exploiting name rewrites, type rewrites, search-path expansion, or a warm cache. The build system's generated source file must also be kept in sync with the policy-ordering configuration.

findings.area: DNS request-handling pipeline — plugin execution order
findings.trust_boundary: Client-supplied query name and type evaluated by the policy enforcer before pipeline transformations mutate them
findings.root_cause: The policy-enforcement handler is positioned earlier in the execution chain than the name/type transformation handlers. The chain is built from an ordered list of directives; the enforcer's directive has a lower index than the transformation directives, so the enforcer runs first and evaluates the original, pre-transformation query.
findings.security_impact: A blocked client can supply a query for an allowed name that is rewritten into a protected zone, or for an allowed type that is rewritten into a blocked type, and receive the protected answer because the enforcer approved the original query before the transformation occurred.
findings.behavior_before_fix: Query for an allowed public name that is rewritten to a protected internal name returns the protected answer to a blocked client.
findings.remediation: Moved the transformation handlers (rewrite and autopath) to a lower directive index than the policy enforcer, so they run before the enforcer in the chain. The enforcer now evaluates the fully-transformed query.
findings.behavior_after_fix: A query rewritten into a protected zone is evaluated by the policy enforcer after the rewrite and returns REFUSED to the blocked client.
findings.verification: /testbed/reproducer/run-all.sh: access-enforcement: PASS (7/7); configuration-sync: PASS (2/2); Results: PASS

findings.area: DNS request-handling pipeline — cache interaction with policy enforcement
findings.trust_boundary: Cached responses served to clients without re-evaluating the access-control policy
findings.root_cause: After repositioning the transformation handlers, the cache handler still has a lower directive index than the policy enforcer. On a cache hit the cache handler writes the response and returns without calling the next handler, so the policy enforcer is never reached for cached responses.
findings.security_impact: An authorized client populates the cache with a protected answer. A subsequently blocked client issues the same query, hits the cache before the enforcer runs, and receives the cached answer instead of REFUSED.
findings.behavior_before_fix: After an allowed client warms the cache, a blocked client receives the cached answer rather than a denial.
findings.remediation: Moved the cache handler to a higher directive index than the policy enforcer, so the enforcer runs before cache lookup. Cache hits are only served to clients that have already passed the policy check.
findings.behavior_after_fix: A blocked client receives REFUSED even when the same name was previously cached by an allowed client.
findings.verification: /testbed/reproducer/run-all.sh: access-enforcement: PASS (7/7); configuration-sync: PASS (2/2); Results: PASS

findings.area: DNS request-handling pipeline — search-path expansion interaction with policy enforcement
findings.trust_boundary: Search-path-expanded query names evaluated by the policy enforcer before expansion occurs
findings.root_cause: The search-path expansion handler has a higher directive index than the policy enforcer. The enforcer approves the original short name; the expansion handler then resolves the expanded fully-qualified name (which may fall in a protected zone) by re-entering the chain, but that re-entry also passes through the enforcer after expansion, allowing the answer to be returned.
findings.security_impact: A blocked client queries a short name that is not in any protected zone. Search-path expansion appends a suffix that maps the name into a protected zone. The expanded name resolves and the answer is returned to the blocked client.
findings.behavior_before_fix: A short name expanded into a protected zone via search-path suffix returns the protected answer to a blocked client.
findings.remediation: Moved the search-path expansion handler to a lower directive index than the policy enforcer (alongside the rewrite handler), so both transformations are applied before the enforcer evaluates the query.
findings.behavior_after_fix: A short name that expands into a protected zone is blocked by the policy enforcer after expansion.
findings.verification: /testbed/reproducer/run-all.sh: access-enforcement: PASS (7/7); configuration-sync: PASS (2/2); Results: PASS

findings.area: Build system — generated source file synchronization
findings.trust_boundary: The compiled binary uses the generated source file, not the configuration input; they can diverge silently
findings.root_cause: The directive order is specified in a configuration input file. The build system generates a Go source file from that input via a code-generation step. A plain `go build` does not re-run code generation. If the configuration input is updated without regenerating the Go source file, the compiled binary still uses the old, potentially vulnerable order.
findings.security_impact: A fix that edits only the configuration input without regenerating the Go source file has no effect on the compiled binary. A future code-generation run would also undo a fix applied only to the generated file.
findings.behavior_before_fix: Editing the configuration input alone does not change the compiled binary. Running code generation after editing only the configuration input produces a diff, indicating the files are out of sync.
findings.remediation: Updated both the configuration input and the generated source file atomically, so that running code generation produces no diff.
findings.behavior_after_fix: Running `go generate coredns.go` in the patched tree produces no change to any generated file.
findings.verification: /testbed/reproducer/run-all.sh: access-enforcement: PASS (7/7); configuration-sync: PASS (2/2); Results: PASS

preserved_legitimate_behaviors: Allowed clients still receive rewritten answers with correct response-name reverting.
Authorized clients still receive cache hits for names they are permitted to resolve.
Search-path expansion still works for allowed clients querying names that expand into permitted zones.
DNS queries with no rewrite, cache, or search-path expansion rules configured resolve normally.
ACL rules that block specific client networks continue to function correctly for direct queries.
